title: Ion channels: patch clamp to structures (Bridge to AI: spiking versus rate neurons)
text:
CHAPTER 5. THE ACTION POTENTIAL
SECTION 5.4. ION CHANNELS: FROM PATCH CLAMP TO STRUCTURES

From conductances to molecules

Hodgkin and Huxley described the membrane in terms of macroscopic conductances: the sodium conductance and potassium conductance of a whole patch of axon. They suspected these conductances arose from discrete sites in the membrane through which ions could pass, but they could not see such sites. Over the next half century, neuroscience, biophysics, molecular biology, and structural biology converged to identify the molecules responsible: ion channels. This is one of the great success stories of reductionist science, connecting an equation to a protein structure, atom by atom.

Evidence for discrete channels

Several lines of evidence in the 1960s and early 1970s suggested that ions cross the membrane through specific protein pores.

- Toxins. Tetrodotoxin (TTX) from pufferfish and saxitoxin from certain marine algae block sodium currents at very low concentrations, without affecting potassium currents. Tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks potassium currents. Such specific, high-affinity block suggests specific binding sites on distinct molecules. Toshio Narahashi and John Moore showed in the early 1960s that TTX blocks sodium conductance in squid axons. By measuring how much radioactive TTX bound to a nerve, researchers estimated the density of sodium channels, which turned out to be fairly low in some unmyelinated nerves (tens of channels per square micrometer) and very high at nodes of Ranvier.
- Selectivity. Bertil Hille, in a series of studies in the late 1960s and early 1970s, measured the permeability of sodium channels to many different ions and molecules of different sizes. He found that sodium channels allowed ions up to a certain size, and he proposed that the channel has a narrow "selectivity filter" of about 0.3 by 0.5 nanometers, lined with oxygen atoms that interact with ions. Potassium channels had a different selectivity pattern. This was strong evidence for a physical pore with defined dimensions.
- Gating currents. In 1973, Clay Armstrong and Francisco Bezanilla, and independently Richard Keynes and Eduardo Rojas, recorded tiny currents that flowed when the membrane voltage was stepped, even when ionic currents were blocked. These were the "gating currents" predicted by Hodgkin and Huxley: the movement of charged parts of the channel protein in the electric field as the channel changes shape.
- Ball and chain. Armstrong and Bezanilla also found that treating the inside of the squid axon with the enzyme pronase (which cuts proteins) removed sodium inactivation while leaving activation intact. This suggested that inactivation is produced by a part of the protein on the inner side of the membrane, which could be cut off. They proposed a "ball and chain" model, in which a tethered particle plugs the open pore from the inside. Later, Toshinori Hoshi, William Zagotta, and Richard Aldrich confirmed a ball-and-chain mechanism for a type of potassium channel inactivation in 1990 using molecular methods.

The patch clamp

The definitive evidence came from a new technique. Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann, working at the Max Planck Institute in Gottingen, developed the patch clamp in the 1970s. In 1976 they published recordings of the current through single ion channels, opened by acetylcholine, in frog muscle membrane.

The idea is simple in principle. A glass pipette with a very fine, polished tip (about 1 micrometer across) is pressed against a cell membrane. The rim of the pipette tip seals against the membrane, isolating a tiny patch that may contain only one or a few channels. The current flowing through that patch, into the pipette, is measured with a sensitive amplifier.

The challenge is noise. A single channel passes a current of only a few picoamperes (1 pA = 10^-12 A). To see such a current, the seal between pipette and membrane must have a very high resistance, so that little current leaks around it. In early experiments the seals were tens of megaohms. In 1980 and 1981 Neher, Sakmann, and colleagues (in a paper by Owen Hamill and colleagues) reported that by applying gentle suction, they could obtain seals with resistances over a gigaohm (10^9 ohms), the "gigaseal." This reduced the noise enough to see single-channel currents clearly, and it also made it possible to rip off patches of membrane for study (inside-out and outside-out patches), or to rupture the patch and record from the whole cell (whole-cell recording). Whole-cell patch clamp recording became the standard method for recording from neurons in brain slices and culture.

Neher and Sakmann received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1991.

The thermal noise of a resistor is a useful way to see why the gigaseal matters. The RMS current noise of a resistor R over bandwidth B is sqrt(4*k*T*B/R), where k is Boltzmann's constant and T is temperature. For R = 10 megaohms and B = 1 kHz at room temperature, this is roughly 1 pA, comparable to a single-channel current. For R = 10 gigaohms, it falls to roughly 0.04 pA. The seal resistance directly determines whether single channels can be resolved.

What single channels look like

Single-channel recordings showed that channels behave like stochastic switches. A channel is either closed (no current) or open (a fixed current, say 2 pA), and it flips between these states at random times. The current through an open channel follows Ohm's law reasonably well: i = gamma * (V - E_rev), where gamma is the single-channel conductance, typically in the range of about 1 to a few hundred picosiemens depending on the channel type. For voltage-gated sodium channels, gamma is on the order of 10 to 20 pS.

The macroscopic currents of Hodgkin and Huxley are the sum of many such random openings. If you record from a patch containing one sodium channel and step the voltage repeatedly, each trial shows the channel opening briefly at a random latency, staying open for a random duration (usually about a millisecond), and then closing (inactivating). No single trial looks like the smooth HH sodium current. But if you average hundreds of trials, the average current rises and decays exactly like the macroscopic current. The HH gating variables are probabilities, and the macroscopic conductance is the expected value of a stochastic process. This is a beautiful example of the law of large numbers in biology.

The durations of open and closed times give information about the channel's kinetic states. If a channel has a single open state and a single closed state, the open times are exponentially distributed. More complex distributions reveal multiple states. Channel kinetics are usually modeled as Markov chains: a set of states (closed, open, inactivated, and so on) with voltage-dependent transition rates. The HH model is a special case of such a Markov model with a particular structure.

Cloning the channels

In 1984, the Japanese biochemist Shosaku Numa and colleagues determined the amino acid sequence of the voltage-gated sodium channel from the electric organ of the electric eel by cloning its gene. The electric organ was used because it is extremely rich in sodium channels; the eel's electric organ is made of modified muscle cells (electrocytes) specialized for generating current, essentially biological batteries stacked in series, the same structure that inspired Volta. The sequence revealed a large protein with four similar repeated domains (I to IV), each containing six membrane-spanning segments (S1 to S6). One segment in each domain, S4, contained a regular pattern of positively charged amino acids (arginine or lysine) at every third position. This was immediately proposed as the voltage sensor: a charged helix that moves in response to changes in membrane voltage, producing the gating current and opening the channel.

In 1987 several groups, including those of Lily and Yuh Nung Jan and of Olaf Pongs, cloned a voltage-gated potassium channel from the fruit fly Drosophila, the Shaker channel (named after the mutant fly that shakes its legs under anesthesia). Shaker is a single domain with six segments; four such subunits come together to form a channel, just as the sodium channel has four domains in one protein. So both channel types share a common fourfold architecture, with the pore formed at the center by the S5 and S6 segments and the loop between them, and the voltage sensors (S1 to S4) at the periphery. Voltage-gated calcium channels have the same four-domain architecture as sodium channels.

Since then, genes for hundreds of ion channels have been identified. The human genome contains many genes for potassium channel subunits alone (on the order of 70 or more, depending on how one counts families), giving neurons an enormous toolkit for shaping their electrical behavior.

Seeing the channel: MacKinnon's structures

In 1998, Roderick MacKinnon and colleagues published the first high-resolution atomic structure of a potassium channel, determined by X-ray crystallography. They used KcsA, a simple potassium channel from the bacterium Streptomyces lividans, which is easier to crystallize than complex mammalian channels. MacKinnon received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2003 (shared with Peter Agre, who discovered water channels, aquaporins).

The KcsA structure answered a long-standing puzzle: how can a potassium channel be both highly selective (it conducts potassium ions about 1,000 times better than sodium ions, even though sodium ions are smaller) and fast (conducting on the order of 10^8 ions per second, close to the rate of free diffusion)?

The answer lies in the selectivity filter, a narrow section of the pore lined by backbone carbonyl oxygen atoms from a conserved sequence of amino acids, often summarized by the "signature sequence" TVGYG (threonine, valine, glycine, tyrosine, glycine). In water, a potassium ion is surrounded by a shell of water molecules whose oxygen atoms point toward it. To enter the filter, the ion must shed its water shell, which costs energy. The carbonyl oxygens in the filter are positioned to mimic the water shell almost exactly for a potassium ion, so the energy cost of dehydration is compensated. A sodium ion, being smaller, cannot interact with all the oxygens at once in the same favorable way, so dehydrating it costs more energy than the filter returns. Hence selectivity. The filter contains several ion binding sites in a row, typically with two potassium ions in the filter at a time separated by water molecules; the repulsion between ions helps push them through, which explains the high rate.

Later, MacKinnon's group solved the structure of a voltage-gated potassium channel (Kv1.2) in 2005, showing the voltage sensor domains and how they are coupled to the pore. Since around 2015, the technique of cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), recognized by the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Jacques Dubochet, Joachim Frank, Richard Henderson), has made it possible to determine structures of large, complex channels, including mammalian and human voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, in different states.

How voltage sensing works

Channels sense voltage through the S4 segment. When the membrane is depolarized, the positively charged S4 helix moves outward through the membrane electric field. This movement is transmitted through a linker to the pore-forming segments, opening a gate at the inner end of the pore. The movement of the charges is what produces gating current. Measurements suggest that the opening of a Shaker potassium channel involves the movement of about 12 to 13 elementary charges across the field, a value that is consistent with the steep voltage dependence of channel opening. The exact nature of S4 motion (a sliding helix, a helical screw, or a combination) was debated for years, and structural studies have increasingly supported models in which S4 moves outward in steps relative to surrounding segments.

From a physics point of view, the steep voltage dependence follows from Boltzmann statistics. If opening involves moving z_g elementary charges across the full membrane voltage, then the ratio of open to closed probability is proportional to exp(z_g * e * V / (k * T)). The open probability is then a sigmoid (logistic) function of voltage:

  P_open(V) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(V - V_half) / k_s))

with slope factor k_s = k*T / (z_g * e), which at room temperature is about 25 mV divided by z_g. Larger gating charge gives a steeper curve. This logistic form is used throughout neuroscience to describe the voltage dependence of channels. Notice that the logistic sigmoid of artificial neural networks has exactly this form. In ion channels, the sigmoid is not a design choice; it comes from statistical physics.

Channelopathies and drugs

Because ion channels are central to excitability, mutations in channel genes cause diseases called channelopathies. Examples include certain forms of epilepsy (for example, mutations in the sodium channel gene SCN1A are a major cause of Dravet syndrome), some inherited cardiac arrhythmias (such as long QT syndrome, caused by mutations in potassium or sodium channel genes in heart cells), periodic paralyses involving muscle channels, and some pain disorders. Mutations in the sodium channel Nav1.7 (gene SCN9A) can cause either extreme pain sensitivity or a congenital inability to feel pain, depending on whether the mutation increases or eliminates function. This finding made Nav1.7 a target for developing new pain drugs.

Many drugs act on ion channels. Local anesthetics like lidocaine block sodium channels, preventing action potentials in pain fibers. Some antiepileptic drugs reduce sodium channel activity. Many toxins from snakes, scorpions, cone snails, spiders, and plants target channels, and these toxins are valuable research tools.

A zoo of channels

Beyond voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, neurons use many other channels, each contributing specific dynamics. A few important ones:

- Voltage-gated calcium channels: open on depolarization; the calcium entering triggers neurotransmitter release at synapses and activates many intracellular signals.
- Calcium-activated potassium channels: open when internal calcium rises, producing afterhyperpolarizations that slow firing. This is a mechanism of spike-frequency adaptation.
- Hyperpolarization-activated cation channels (HCN channels, carrying the current I_h): open when the membrane is hyperpolarized, and contribute to rhythmic pacemaking in heart and brain.
- A-type potassium channels: rapidly activating and inactivating, which delay firing and shape dendritic signals.
- Ligand-gated channels: opened by neurotransmitters, such as AMPA and NMDA glutamate receptors, GABA-A receptors, and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (chapter 6).
- Mechanosensitive channels: opened by stretch or pressure; the Piezo channels, discovered by Ardem Patapoutian and colleagues, are central to touch and proprioception. The 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian for discoveries of receptors for temperature and touch.
- Temperature-sensitive channels: the TRP channels such as TRPV1, which responds to heat and to capsaicin, the compound that makes chili peppers hot (discovered by Julius's lab).

Each neuron type expresses a particular combination of channels, which gives it a characteristic firing pattern: regular spiking, fast spiking, bursting, adapting, and so on.

Bridge to AI: stochastic units, sigmoids, and the diversity of units

Three ideas from this section have interesting counterparts in AI.

Stochastic switching. Single channels are random two-state devices whose average behavior is smooth and deterministic. In AI, randomness is also used deliberately. Dropout, a regularization technique introduced by Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues around 2012, randomly switches off units during training, which can make networks more robust. Boltzmann machines and other stochastic neural networks use units that switch on and off randomly with probabilities given by a logistic function of their input, the same mathematics as a voltage-gated channel's open probability. And there is a line of research on stochastic computing and probabilistic hardware that uses noisy devices to perform sampling-based inference.

The physical origin of the sigmoid. The logistic sigmoid used in early neural networks and in gating units of LSTMs is exactly the Boltzmann distribution for a two-state system. In channels, it arises naturally from thermodynamics. This is a reminder that some "design choices" in AI have deep physical roots.

Unit diversity. Artificial networks typically use the same activation function for every unit. Brains use a wide diversity of neuron types, each with a different combination of channels and thus different input-output dynamics. Some researchers have explored networks with heterogeneous units, for example with learnable time constants or learnable activation functions, and have reported advantages in some tasks, particularly for processing signals with structure on multiple time scales. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, proposed in 2024, place learnable functions on the connections rather than fixed activation functions on the units, which is a different route to richer, more diverse nonlinearities. Whether biological diversity is a computational resource, an evolutionary accident, or a necessity for metabolic and developmental reasons is an open and interesting question.

Summary

- Toxins, selectivity studies, gating currents, and protease experiments in the 1960s and 1970s suggested that ions pass through specific protein channels with gates and filters.
- Neher and Sakmann's patch clamp (1976, with the gigaseal around 1980 and 1981) allowed recording of currents through single channels, earning the 1991 Nobel Prize.
- Single channels are stochastic switches; macroscopic HH currents are averages of many random openings, and channel kinetics are described by Markov models.
- Cloning (sodium channel 1984, Shaker potassium channel 1987) revealed fourfold architectures with S4 voltage sensors.
- MacKinnon's 1998 KcsA structure explained potassium selectivity and speed; cryo-EM now reveals complex channel structures.
- Voltage dependence follows a Boltzmann sigmoid, the same function used in artificial neurons; channel diversity gives neurons diverse dynamics.
